name: Spirited Away
blurb: Miyazaki's film about a girl who must work in a bathhouse for spirits to save her parents
title: Spirited Away Explained: Plot Summary and Ending
description: Spirited Away explained: who Chihiro, Haku, Yubaba and No-Face are, the story from the tunnel to the pig test, what the ending means, and the film's themes.
h1: Spirited Away: Plot Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Spirited Away is a 2001 Japanese animated film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki and made by Studio Ghibli. It opened in Japan on 20 July 2001 and runs 124 minutes. Ten-year-old Chihiro Ogino, sulking over a move to a new town, wanders with her parents through a tunnel into an abandoned-looking place that turns out to be a town of spirits and gods. To rescue her parents and find her way home, she has to work in a great bathhouse run by a witch, and the film follows how a timid child learns to fend for herself.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: A ten-year-old girl who ends up in the spirit world while moving house
A mysterious boy who works for Yubaba and helps Chihiro
The witch who owns and runs the bathhouse
Yubaba's twin sister, who lives far away
The many-armed old man who runs the bathhouse boiler room
A young bathhouse worker who looks after Chihiro
A silent, masked spirit who follows Chihiro
Akio and Yūko Ogino, who are driving the family to their new home

body: Beginning. On the way to their new house, Chihiro's father takes a wrong turn up a forest road that ends at a tunnel. Beyond it lies what looks like an empty theme park. Her parents find a stall laid out with food and start eating without asking. Chihiro wanders off, sees a huge bathhouse and meets a boy, Haku, who tells her to leave before dark. Night falls, spirits appear, and she finds her parents have been turned into pigs. The way back is now a sea.

Middle. Haku tells her that to survive she must get a job. She asks the boiler man Kamaji, who sends her with the worker Lin to Yubaba at the top of the bathhouse. Yubaba gives her a contract and takes her name, leaving her only Sen. Haku warns her that Yubaba controls people by stealing their names, and that he has forgotten his own; he gives Chihiro back the card her friends wrote so she will remember hers. Chihiro is given the dirtiest jobs. She bathes a foul-smelling guest whom everyone else avoids and pulls a mass of rubbish out of him; he is really a polluted river spirit, and he rewards her with a herbal dumpling. She had earlier let No-Face in from the rain. He starts handing out gold, swallows workers and grows monstrous, until Chihiro feeds him part of the dumpling and he throws up everything he ate.

Meanwhile Haku, in the form of a white dragon, is wounded by paper birds sent by Zeniba after he stole her magic golden seal on Yubaba's orders. Chihiro gives him the rest of the dumpling, and he coughs up the seal and a black slug, a spell Yubaba used to control him. To return the seal and apologise, Chihiro rides a train across the water to Zeniba's cottage, with No-Face and Boh, whom Zeniba's magic has turned into a mouse. Zeniba turns out to be kind and gives Chihiro a hair tie woven by her companions.

End. Haku arrives to carry her home. As they fly, Chihiro remembers that as a little girl she fell into the Kohaku River and was carried safely to the bank. Haku is the spirit of that river, whose real name is Nigihayami Kohakunushi; the river was later filled in and built over. Hearing his name, Haku is freed. At the bathhouse Yubaba sets a final test: pick out her parents from a pen of pigs. Chihiro says none of them are her parents. She is right, the contract vanishes and she is free. Haku walks her to the edge of the spirit world and tells her not to look back until she is through the tunnel.

Chihiro walks back through the tunnel with her parents, who remember nothing and are surprised to find the car covered in leaves and dust, as if much time has passed. She hesitates and looks back at the tunnel, and the hair tie from Zeniba glints in her hair, proof that what happened was real. Haku has promised they will meet again, but the film never shows whether they do, and Haku has said he intends to quit his apprenticeship and face Yubaba.

The film does not state whether Chihiro will remember the spirit world. Zeniba says that nothing that happens is ever forgotten, even if you cannot remember it, which many viewers take as the answer: she may forget the details but keep what she learned. The test with the pigs is often read as the clearest sign of her change: the girl who could not get out of a car without complaining now sees through a trick on her own.

Miyazaki's planning notes say he wanted to make a film for girls of about ten, showing a girl rediscovering the strength to live, and showing that words and names are a person's will and identity. He has said the parents turning into pigs stands for human greed, linked to the excess of Japan's bubble-economy years. Other readings, which Miyazaki has not confirmed, see the bathhouse as a picture of modern work and the polluted river spirit as a comment on the environment.

ul: Names and identity: Yubaba controls workers by taking their names, and both Chihiro and Haku are saved by remembering who they are.
Growing up: Chihiro begins scared and sulky and ends brave, hardworking and kind, without ever gaining special powers.
Greed: her parents' gorging, and No-Face's gold that makes the workers grab and fawn, show what wanting too much does to people.
Nature and pollution: the stink spirit choked with rubbish and Haku's buried river show what people do to the natural world.
Kindness and work: Chihiro wins over Lin, Kamaji and Zeniba by honest effort and courtesy rather than cleverness.
Runtime: 124 minutes; original language Japanese, with an English dub produced under Pixar's John Lasseter.
Original story by Miyazaki, not adapted from a book; Joe Hisaishi wrote the music.
Recognition: it shared the Golden Bear at the 2002 Berlin film festival and won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.
Content advisory: suitable for most children, though some scenes, such as the parents' transformation and No-Face's rampage, can frighten young viewers.

check.q: What happens to Chihiro's parents after they eat the spirits' food?
check.why: Her parents gorge on food meant for the spirits and are turned into pigs.

options: A human boy who got lost
The spirit of the Kohaku River
check.why: Chihiro remembers falling into the Kohaku River as a child, and Haku is its spirit.

check.q: How does Chihiro pass Yubaba's final test?
options: She says none of the pigs are her parents
She picks the two smallest pigs
check.why: Her parents are not among the pigs at all, and she sees through the trick.

faq.q: Do Chihiro and Haku ever meet again?
faq.a: The film does not say. Haku promises they will, and the ending leaves it open; no sequel exists.

faq.q: Why can't Chihiro look back in the tunnel?
faq.a: Haku tells her not to look back until she is out. The film gives no reason, but it echoes old myths in which looking back means losing the way home, and it marks her leaving the spirit world for good.

No-Face seems lonely and takes on the moods of whoever he swallows. Chihiro was kind to him without wanting his gold, and he attaches himself to her; at the end he stays with Zeniba, who gives him something to do.
